8.0.s.en: 1. The victory of Assyria over Syria and Israel:

8.0.0.en: 1 Moreover the LORD said unto me, “Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man's pen concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 2 And that I take unto me faithful witnesses to record, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.” 3 And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 4 For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.”

8.0.1.en: In the previous chapter the Lord spoke with Ahaz, who was trembling before Syria and Israel; now He speaks with the people, affirming the ruin of the two kingdoms that had allied together against Judah. By divine command Isaiah took a great tablet and wrote on it in clear letters “Maher-shalal-hash-baz,” which means “Hasten to the spoil, hurry to the plunder.” The prophet Isaiah placed the tablet in a visible place in the temple so that everyone might read it, and two priests witnessed to it, Uriah and Zechariah. Uriah was a high priest in the days of Ahaz, his spiritual counselor and his partner in pagan worship. He had built an altar like the altar of the Syrians that Hezekiah saw in Damascus, so that the king might offer sacrifices upon it (2 Kgs 16:10-16).

8.0.2.en: The two priests signed the tablet, or sealed it with their two seals, as trustworthy witnesses, for in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established (2 Cor 13:1); they bore witness that what he wrote was written before the event occurred.

8.1.0.en: The prophet Isaiah declares that when his son Maher-shalal-hash-baz is about one year old, the prophecy against Syria and Israel will be fulfilled, saying: “Before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria” [4]. This was accomplished by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29; 16:9; 1 Chr 5:26).

8.2.s.en: 2. A warning to the people of Judah:

8.2.0.en: 5 The LORD spake also unto me again, saying, 6 “Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son; 7 Now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory: and he shall come up over all his channels, and go over all his banks: 8 And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.”

8.2.1.en: After God had declared His salvation of the city of Jerusalem by shattering Syria and Israel, who had allied against it, He began to recount the sins of the people of Judah and the chastenings that would come upon them. Although He defends them, He does not defend their sins, nor does He cover them up, but He asks for repentance from them and a return to Him.

8.3.0.en: He says: “Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son” [6]. “Shiloah” is a watercourse whose name means “Sent,” and which is called “Siloam” in the New Testament. This channel was cut in the rock; it is several thousand feet long and lies southwest of Jerusalem. The waters flow in it quietly, the city depends on it, and it was a symbol of the house of David. What does it mean that the people refused the waters of this channel? They compared it with the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, and so they rejected it and despised it. This points to their disdain for what God had given them, “the kingdom of Judah,” as they looked to what others had, “human arms.” They lost their faith in God, the giver of victory, and feared Rezin and the son of Remaliah, strangers and enemies of Judah, taking refuge in anyone who would rescue them from the two.

8.3.1.en: The waters of Shiloah point to the power of the quiet and meek Spirit, the source of sanctification and the fountain of righteousness.

8.3.2.en: Also “Shiloah” means “Sent,” pointing to the Lord Christ, whom the Father sent for our salvation, and whom the Jews rejected, refusing the work of His Holy Spirit.

8.4.0.en: They rejected the quiet watercourse and sought overwhelming, mighty waters, so the Lord chastens them by bringing up upon them “the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory” [7]. If Judah leans on Assyria, he will indeed come and save it, but afterward he turns and pours over it like the river Euphrates that they admired and desired, overflowing Judah and drowning it [7]. Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian rescued Judah, but Sennacherib the Assyrian attacked Judah with force and reached the neck, and besieged the head, Jerusalem, which was about to fall had God not intervened: “He shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings (the two branches of the Euphrates) shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel” [8].

8.4.1.en: Thus God allows chastening, and trials come like a sweeping flood until they reach our necks, but He keeps the head (our faith in the Lord Christ, our Head) above the floods of trials, so that our faith does not fail and we perish (Lk 22:32), because we are the land of Immanuel, the possession of the Lord.

8.4.2.en: St. Augustine comments on the words of the Lord Christ, “Be ye therefore wise as serpents” (Mt 10:16), saying: [We must imitate the wisdom of the serpent, which puts its head between its coils when danger surrounds it, so that the blows fall on the body and not on the head, knowing that it will not perish as long as its head is safe. So it is fitting for us to keep our faith in the Lord Christ, our Head, unharmed, whatever afflictions come upon us, and then we will not perish.]

8.5.0.en: However much the enemy of good tries to stretch out his wings within us [8], no harm will touch us as long as our whole land is the land of Immanuel, that is, as long as our life is hidden under the shadow of the Lord's wings, as long as we carry within us the Kingdom of Christ!

8.6.0.en: 9 Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries: gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces; gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces. 10 Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.

8.6.1.en: While the prophet is speaking about the events of his own time, behold, the Lord lifts his eyes and the eyes of the believers toward the saving work of Christ. God in His love is gentle with the people of Judah, so He saves them from the alliance of Syria and Israel against them, and at the same time, since the people sin by taking refuge in Assyria, Assyria itself becomes their opponent. This is what God permitted, but He did not permit the complete destruction of Judah, because from it comes the Lord Christ, the Lion that comes out of the tribe of Judah. He permits the Assyrian invasion to overflow as far as the neck of Judah, but it does not touch the head, for the Word of God becomes incarnate from the tribe of Judah, from St. Mary, and Immanuel dwells among us, who makes of our hearts a land, or a kingdom, for Himself... This is what moved the prophet to pass suddenly from the problem of Judah in the prophet's time, or shortly after it, to speak of the powers allied against Immanuel, saying:

8.6.2.en: “Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and make, all ye of far countries. Gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces. Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us” [9-10].

8.6.3.en: The matter did not stop with Assyria, which collapsed when 185,000 of its men died in the battle, but the prophet announces the fall of all the powers of the world that oppose the truth: Assyria, followed by Babylon, then Persia and Media and the Roman Empire (Isa 54:17; Mic 4:13). And all the more he meant the spiritual powers of darkness that oppose the Kingdom of Christ. The prophet announces that the raging of the enemies, their alliance and their wicked counsels against the Church are directed against Immanuel who dwells in her midst; therefore the powers of darkness collapse, and the true Church enjoys victory.

8.6.4.en: This prophetic voice cries out against all who oppose Christ, proclaiming what the Lord Himself said to Saul: “Why persecutest thou me...? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:4-5). Let the enemy do all he can in opposing the believers; he only shatters himself.

8.7.0.en: 11 For the LORD spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying, 12 “Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. 13 Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. 14 And he shall be for a sanctuary, and for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. 15 And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken.”

8.7.1.en: It seems that some did not believe the words of the prophet and reckoned them a political conspiracy or national treason and opposition to the king and the authorities, so that Judah should not take refuge in Assyria and perish at the hands of the Syrians and Israel. The Lord took hold of Isaiah, as it were by the hand, to strengthen him [11]. Some see that Isaiah himself, as a man, sometimes inclined to the opinion of the king and his counselors and the people, but God insisted on making the way clear to him even though it was contrary to the opinion of the community; it is as though He took him by the hand to lead him into the narrow, rejected way. Perhaps the Lord took him by the hand to strengthen him because of the false accusations made against him, and so that he would not cease his prophetic work because of what these people stirred up, but He wants him to strengthen the faithful hands by their sanctification to the Lord. It is as though the Lord holds the hands of Isaiah so that the latter in turn may hold the hands of the faithful and place them in the hands of the holy God. Therefore He says: “Neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” [12-13]. Every faithful soul in the service of the Lord is opposed, but the Lord Himself supports it, not only that it may work but that it may support others and encourage them to work in the Spirit of God, looking not at the opposition but at the support of the Lord of hosts for them.

8.7.2.en: How wonderful are these words: “Fear not... sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.” The evil powers have united and allied in arrogance and pride, but the children of God unite together in the Lord, they unite under the leadership of the holy Lord of hosts in love and sanctification. These do not lean on human arms and do not want an alliance between light and darkness, but believe in overcoming and victory through sanctification, or fellowship with the holy God.

8.8.0.en: It is not Isaiah alone who is opposed, nor the faithful believers alone, but “Immanuel” Himself becomes an object of opposition and a stone of stumbling to many: “And he shall be for a sanctuary, and for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken” [14-15].

8.8.1.en: He is a “sanctuary,” or a “holy stone,” for the believers who take refuge in Him and hold fast to Him for their protection and salvation; He is the “foundation stone” and the “cornerstone” that joins the believers from the Jews with the believers from the Gentiles like two walls that meet together in Him. At the same time He is a stone of stumbling and offence to unbelievers.

8.8.2.en: * Whenever (Christ) is presented in Holy Scripture as a stone, He is a stone of stumbling to unbelievers and a foundation stone to believers (Isa 8:14; 28:16; Dan 2:34, 45; Mt 21:44; Lk 20:17; Acts 5:11; Rom 9:33, etc.).

8.8.3.en: St. Augustine The Lord Christ came to His own and His own received Him not, therefore He says “a rock of offence to my house”; what increases His wounds is that the rejection is from His own house.

8.8.4.en: St. Peter quoted this prophecy (1 Pet 2:8), declaring its fulfillment in the person of the Lord Christ.

8.9.0.en: 16 “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples. 17 And I will wait upon the LORD, that hideth his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him. 18 Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the LORD of hosts, which dwelleth in mount Zion.”

8.9.1.en: Although the Lord Christ's own, or the people of His house, rejected Him so that He became a stone of stumbling to them, there was found a holy remnant that received Him, such as the disciples and the apostles and the Marys and the house of Lazarus, and so on... This remnant is reckoned a holy leaven which the Spirit of God uses to leaven the dough in the whole world.

8.9.2.en: What happened with the Lord Christ took place with Isaiah in a faint image, since he was a type of Christ, for he too had faithful disciples.

8.9.3.en: “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples” [16]. The holy few received the words of the prophet Isaiah as true prophecies and a divine word, reckoning his words a declaration of the mind of God and His holy will. These the prophet called his disciples and also “the children whom the LORD hath given me” [8]. These must seal or bind up what they heard, for these prophecies must be kept safe until the times of the New Testament, when they are revealed to simple children (Mt 11:25). Sealing them also means the obligation not to add to them or take away from them.

8.10.0.en: What Isaiah mentioned seemed in his time an impossible matter that had to be resisted; for this reason he and his disciples had to arm themselves with patience for the Lord [17]. They lived in an oppressive atmosphere: the Lord was hiding His face from His people [17], as though they were not His people and He did not know them, delivering them over to their rejected and ruined minds, a matter that grieved the heart of Isaiah and his disciples; and at the same time the people looked at them as strangers and oddities, full of folly. So by his saying, “Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the LORD of hosts” [18], he means that Isaiah and his disciples were like signs and wonders to the people, since they differed from everyone in their faith, their conduct and their thoughts toward the Lord.

8.10.1.en: Isaiah's disciples were reckoned as his children, and in this he bears a type of the Lord Christ, who longs to bind the believers in Him with a unique bond, like the bond of a father with his children.

8.11.0.en: * He is a brother and friend and bridegroom: “Henceforth I call you not servants... but I have called you friends” (Jn 15:15). And Paul says: “I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2); “that he might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom 8:29). We are no longer only His brothers but have become His children, for He says: “Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me” [18]; not only this, but we have become His members and His body.

8.11.1.en: * Here (Heb 2:13; Isa 8:18) (Christ) shows Himself a father as He showed Himself earlier a brother.

8.11.2.en: St. John Chrysostom * [He is speaking with those seeking baptism.]

8.11.3.en: * The angels share your joy, and Christ Himself, the Great High Priest... presents you all to the Father, saying: “Behold I and the children which God hath given me,” that He may keep you all the object of the delight of His gaze.

8.11.4.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem As the prophet Isaiah presents his disciples to God as witnesses of the truth, a type of the person of the Lord Christ, who presents His believers to the Father as members of His body and sons of the truth, the delight of the Father, so it is fitting for us also to care for everyone, especially the members of the family, that we may present them to God as His beloved. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us think seriously about our wives and our children and our servants, realizing that by this we establish for ourselves a good (easy) order, and our dealings with them become gentle and tender.]

8.12.0.en: 19 And when they shall say unto you, “Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter,” “Should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” 20 To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. 21 And they shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: and it shall come to pass, that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and look upward. 22 And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness.

8.12.1.en: The people felt as though God had hidden His face from them, so they began to demand that the officials, perhaps including some of Isaiah's disciples, resort to those who have familiar spirits and to soothsayers, to seek counsel and to learn about future matters. The prophet calls them those “that peep and that mutter” [19], because they speak in a low voice, as though from another world, to perfect the playing of their part.

8.12.2.en: What does resorting to divination mean? It is a person's loss of every refuge or help, as happened with King Saul. He felt that he was isolated from God and from His prophets, and even the people had withdrawn from him, so he resorted to the dead, asking them through the woman who practiced divination.

8.13.0.en: It was fitting for the people of Judah, leaders and people, to resort to God and consult His prophets and hear the word of God that gives light in the midst of the darkness [20], and so receive good counsel and knowledge of the will of God and help and grace; but when they resort to divination in all its forms and to asking the dead, this means that they lifted their eyes upward and found heaven angry [21], and looked toward the earth and behold, thick darkness had settled upon it.

8.13.1.en: In brief, the people of Judah fell into two grave sins: resorting to human alliances instead of relying on God, and returning to divination and the dead instead of enjoying the living word of God that gives enlightenment and strength.

8.13.2.en: This painful picture proclaims an important truth: the need for a divine Savior!
